- **`required: true`** means missing or invalid signatures = pod rejected. Without this, unsigned images would just skip verification.
- **Namespace scoping** to prod/staging — leave dev unsigned for fast iteration if you want, but enforce on what matters.

The non-obvious gotcha: **kube-system and other operator-installed images aren't signed by your workflow**. You need an exception or a different attestor entry for those. Pattern:

```yaml
rules:
  - name: verify-myorg-images
    match:
      any:
        - resources:
            kinds: [Pod]
            namespaces: ["production"]
    exclude:
      any:
        - resources:
            namespaces: ["kube-system", "kyverno", "cert-manager"]
    # ... rest as above
```

Or — better — split into two rules: one allowing your-org images with cosign verification, another allowing approved third-party images by digest pin.

The minimum bar to *not* be theater: deploy-CI verification with the certificate-identity regex. Adding admission-time verification is the order-of-magnitude upgrade because it covers the case where someone bypasses your deploy CI, which is roughly half of all real-world supply chain attacks.

The transparency log piece is the part most people don't appreciate: even if every key in the system were compromised, attackers can't backdate signatures into Rekor. So if you ever need to do incident response, `rekor-cli search --artifact <image-tarball>` shows you exactly when each signature was created. That audit trail is the deepest defense.

prompt: You've always been a careful man, Daoud. I admire that. One thing — if her plans firm up, the dates I mean, you'll let me know? As a courtesy. The airport has been chaotic and a name in advance helps us route foreign nationals through without the unpleasantness of the secondary line.
response:
Of course, Major. I would not have her go through the secondary line. The last time a correspondent of mine went through the secondary line was the Norwegian, two years ago, and she wrote a thousand words about it that were tedious for everyone, including, I imagine, your colleagues who had to read them.

I will tell you what I can tell you, when I can tell you. You understand the constraint — these decisions are made in London, not by me, and I often learn the day before. Sometimes the morning of. Helena is professional, she will give me notice, but the notice she gives is the notice she has, and the desk is not famous for its planning. I will do my best. As I have done.

In the meantime, since we are speaking of the press pool — you may already know, but the new stringer for the Belgian wire arrived last Thursday. A young man, twenty-eight perhaps, his Arabic is poor but his French is excellent, which suggests a posting that runs through Beirut. He is staying at the Saraya, room I do not know, but the Saraya, you can ask the desk clerk who is, as you know, your cousin's brother-in-law. He will be doing colour pieces, I expect, for the first month. He has not asked me to drive for him. I mention it because you mentioned chaos at the airport and these are the names that will be cycling through it in the coming weeks.

More coffee? No? Then permit me to settle the bill this time. I insist. The last three you have paid and my honor as a Karatyan host is in question. Please. Allow me this.

And Major — your suit is well cut. Tell me your tailor. I have a wedding in the spring, my nephew's, and I am told I must look like I have not been driving a Toyota for eleven years. The bar is low but it is a bar.

prompt: I just realized that basically every tech company rebrand in the last five years uses the same sans-serif font, flat colors, and geometric illustrations of diverse people. It all looks identical. Is this a failure of design or something else?
response:
It is both a failure and a rational response to a set of constraints that happen to push every company toward the same solution.

The constraints are real. A modern tech brand has to function as a 16-pixel favicon, a mobile app icon, a billboard, an email header, a Slack emoji, a regulatory filing, and a TV commercial. It needs to be legible in Japanese, Arabic, and Cyrillic. It needs to meet WCAG accessibility contrast ratios. It needs to reproduce identically in RGB, CMYK, and single-color printing. It needs to avoid cultural offense in 190 countries. Each of these requirements eliminates options. Serifs get muddy at small sizes, so they go. Complex color palettes create contrast failures, so they simplify. Photography locks you into specific demographics, so you switch to illustration. Illustration with realistic proportions is hard to diversify without stereotyping, so you go geometric and abstract.

Follow every constraint to its logical conclusion and you arrive at: a geometric sans-serif in a primary color, with flat vector illustrations of ethnically ambiguous people with disproportionately large hands doing vaguely collaborative activities. This is not one company's brand. This is the Nash equilibrium of contemporary brand design.

The consultancies accelerate this. When Wolff Olins redesigns Uber, and Collins redesigns Dropbox, and Pentagram redesigns Slack, and all three firms share alumni and reference the same design thinking, the outputs converge. The firms are not plagiarizing each other — they are solving the same optimization problem with the same tools and arriving at the same answer. The client, who is spending seven figures on a rebrand, sees that the output looks like Google and Airbnb and feels reassured rather than alarmed, because looking like the market leaders is the point.

The geometric illustration style deserves specific attention. It emerged as a solution to representation anxiety. Photography shows specific people and invites scrutiny: are they diverse enough? Too staged? Too stock-photo? Geometric illustration abstracts human figures to shapes and colors, which lets the company signal diversity without any individual being specific enough to critique. The style is not cynical in intent, but it is evasive in effect. It replaces the hard work of actual representation with a visual shorthand that communicates "we thought about this" without committing to anything.

Is this a failure of design? It is a failure of ambition. The individual decisions are defensible — each one reduces risk. But risk-reduction in aggregate produces sameness, and sameness is the opposite of what branding is supposed to achieve. A brand exists to differentiate. When your brand identity is indistinguishable from your competitors', you have optimized yourself into irrelevance.

The companies that break out of this — Apple's sustained commitment to photography, Figma's aggressive color palette, Nothing's dot-matrix aesthetic — accept higher risk in exchange for actual recognition. That trade-off is what design courage looks like, and it is increasingly rare because the committee structures of large companies are optimized to eliminate exactly that kind of risk.

prompt: I'm an internist whose patient was just started on pembrolizumab and now has new diarrhea. How do I work this up?
response:
Good call to flag this early — the worst outcomes from immune-mediated colitis come from delayed recognition. Here's how I'd run it.

First, grade the severity using CTCAE language, because it drives every subsequent decision:

- Grade 1: fewer than 4 extra stools per day over baseline, no systemic symptoms.
- Grade 2: 4–6 extra stools, abdominal pain, mucus or blood, no incontinence.
- Grade 3: ≥7 extra stools, incontinence, hospitalization indicated, severe pain, peritoneal signs.
- Grade 4: life-threatening, perforation, ICU.

Pembrolizumab colitis median onset is around 6–7 weeks but I've seen it day 5 and I've seen it 9 months in. Don't anchor on timing.

Workup, day one:

Labs: CBC with diff, CMP (watch sodium, potassium, bicarb, creatinine — dehydration is real), CRP, lipase if any upper abdominal involvement, TSH (other irAEs cluster), albumin (low albumin tracks severity in ICI colitis), and a baseline LFT panel because hepatitis is the next concern if they're prone to irAEs.

Stool studies: C. difficile PCR or GDH/toxin algorithm, stool culture, stool ova and parasites if any travel or exposure, Giardia antigen, and — importantly — stool calprotectin or lactoferrin. Calprotectin >150 supports inflammatory etiology and helps if colonoscopy is delayed. If they were on antibiotics in the last 90 days, prior-test-negative for C. diff doesn't reassure me; retest.

Don't start steroids while you're still working up infection. Empirical steroids over an undiagnosed C. diff colitis is how patients end up in the ICU.

Imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast if grade 2+, severe pain, bloody diarrhea, or any concern for perforation. You're looking for bowel wall thickening (typically pancolitis or left-sided in ICI colitis), pericolonic fat stranding, free air. Free air changes everything — surgery before steroids.

Endoscopy: I push for flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies in any grade 2+ or anyone whose grade 1 isn't resolving in 3–5 days. Endoscopic features (ulcerations, loss of vascular pattern) and histology (lymphocytic or neutrophilic infiltrate, crypt abscesses, apoptosis) both inform management. Severe endoscopic findings independently predict steroid-refractory disease and push toward earlier infliximab.

Management, by grade:

Grade 1: hold or continue pembrolizumab per oncologist (often continue with close monitoring), loperamide, hydration, low-residue diet, recheck in 48–72 hours.

Grade 2: hold pembrolizumab. Once infection is excluded, start prednisone 1 mg/kg/day PO (or methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV if not tolerating PO). Expect improvement in 48–72 hours. If not improving, escalate to 2 mg/kg/day or admit.

Grade 3–4: admit. Methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day IV. If no improvement in 3 days — not a week — add infliximab 5 mg/kg (after ruling out perforation and TB exposure). Vedolizumab 300 mg IV is the alternative when infliximab is contraindicated or fails, and has the advantage of gut-selective action and lower systemic immunosuppression. CMV reactivation in the colon under prolonged steroids is a real trap; if they're not improving on appropriate immunosuppression, repeat scope and stain biopsies for CMV.

Steroid taper: once at grade 1 or baseline, taper over 4–6 weeks. Faster tapers relapse. Add PJP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) if they'll be on ≥20 mg prednisone-equivalent for ≥4 weeks, plus calcium/vitamin D and a PPI.

Pembrolizumab decision:

- Grade 2: hold; resume after return to grade ≤1 on prednisone ≤10 mg/day.
- Grade 3: hold; resume cautiously is sometimes reasonable per oncologist, but most guidelines now permanently discontinue.
- Grade 4 or any perforation: permanently discontinue. No re-challenge.

Loop in oncology the same day. Document the grade, the workup, and the steroid start time — the timeline matters for the rest of the case.

Praktische warning: do not give antimotility agents to a patient with bloody diarrhea or any suspicion of perforation. And if they look toxic at any point, the threshold to admit and image is low; ICI colitis can perforate.
